ta-l1d18q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 18, which treats the name that fits the Spirit by reason of his temporal procession, 'gift'. Lombard treats 'gift' as said of the Spirit in comparison with other gifts, and then 'gift' (donum) as compared with 'given' (datum). He asks whether both are said of the Spirit for the same reason and answers that the Spirit is called both gift and given, showing their difference first as to what is in the gift and then as to whose gift it is. In a gift two things are considered: the relation or property by which it is called gift, and the procession from which that character follows in our understanding. On the side of relation, the Spirit is called gift by the same notion by which he is called Holy Spirit; on the side of procession, by the procession by which he is gift he has the divine essence, but not as given. The Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given. As eternally gift he is referred to Father and Son, and Lombard asks whether the Son, being given to us, is called 'ours', and whether the Spirit is referred to himself, deferring the latter. Five articles are announced: whether 'gift' is essential or personal, whether it is proper to the Spirit, whether all gifts are given through this gift, whether by the procession by which he is gift the Spirit is also God, and whether he can be called 'our gift'.
claims: The Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given.
He is called gift by the same notion by which he is called Holy Spirit.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3541.summary: First argument that 'gift' is an essential name. Every name connoting an effect in creatures signifies the divine essence, and 'gift' connotes such an effect, since the Spirit is called gift as givable to creatures in some effect.
claims: Names connoting effects in creatures are essential.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3544.summary: Second argument. No personal name fits the essence, since the essence neither begets nor is begotten, but the divine essence is said to be given to the Son by the Father ('he gave him the name above every name', Phil. 2:9; Hilary). So 'gift' is essential.
claims: The essence is said to be given to the Son.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3550.summary: Third argument. The Spirit is gift insofar as he proceeds as love, and love in God is also said essentially (Augustine, Dist. 10), so 'gift' is too.
claims: Love is said essentially in God.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3554.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is had from another is given. Even without understanding the distinction of persons, we could have God for enjoyment, and we do not have this from ourselves, so it would be given. Whatever is understood in God when the distinction of persons is excluded is essential.
claims: What remains when the persons are abstracted is essential.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3557.summary: Sed contra. Whatever belongs to a person by reason of origin is notional, not essential, and the Spirit is called gift insofar as he proceeds eternally, as Lombard says.
claims: What belongs by origin is notional.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3560.summary: Thomas's determination. As explained in Distinction 15, giving is said in two ways: of what is had by lordship, like a possession, or of what is had as intrinsic, as one has oneself, one's matter, or a quality. Although there is no lordship of one divine person over another, there is authority of principle. So giving can imply authority over what is given, and then 'gift' or 'given' is notional. Or it can imply no authority, only that what is given is had freely, and in this way the essence itself is said to be given, so that 'gift' is essential rather than personal. It always implies a distinction of giver from recipient, though not from what is given.
claims: 'Gift' is notional when it implies the giver's authority of origin, essential when it implies only free possession.
Giving always implies distinction of giver and recipient, not of giver and gift.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3563.summary: Reply to the first argument. A name can connote an effect in creatures in two ways. Only by way of principle: then, since the whole Trinity's operation is one, the name is common to the Trinity and essential. Or with something else besides the principle relative to creatures: then, though by the relation to creatures it gives one to understand the essence consequently, as a cause is understood in its effect, by the other thing it signifies it can belong to a person. 'To assume flesh', for example, implies an operation common to the three persons and the terminus of the assumption, which is proper to the Son. Likewise 'gift', besides its relation to the one to whom it is givable, implies a relation to the one from whom it is, as from a principle having authority over it, and in this respect it is notional.
claims: 'Gift' connotes an effect in creatures but also implies relation to a principle with authority, which makes it notional.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3566.summary: Reply to the second argument. If giving implies authority in the giver over what is given, the essence is not said to be given in that sense, only in the other sense.
claims: The essence is given only in the sense without authority.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3569.summary: Reply to the third argument, following from the above. Essential love, though it has the character of first gift in which other gifts are given, admits no authority over it, so it cannot be said to be given in the sense implying the giver's authority.
claims: Essential love is not 'given' in the notional sense.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3573.summary: Reply to the fourth argument, likewise. The gift whose concept implies authority does not remain when the distinction of persons is not understood.
claims: Notional gift disappears when the persons are abstracted.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3585.summary: First argument that 'gift' is not proper to the Spirit. The Spirit's temporal procession or mission is called his giving, and the Son is sent like the Spirit and has aptitude for mission from his eternal procession (Dist. 15). So the Son could be called gift like the Spirit.
claims: The Son is also sent and given.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3588.summary: Second argument. Since persons are distinguished by eternal processions, a person's proper name can be expressed in the act of procession, as 'Son' is in generation. 'Gift' is not expressed in the eternal procession, since the Father is not said to 'give' a gift as he is said to beget a son.
claims: Proper names are expressed in the act of procession.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3591.summary: Third argument. The properties of the persons signify only relation, since the persons are not distinguished in absolutes. 'Gift' signifies not only a relation but also something given.
claims: Personal properties signify only relations.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3595.summary: Fourth argument. The Spirit has only one notion, his procession, but he is known in one way as gift and another as proceeding, so the notion by which he is called gift is not proper to him.
claims: The Spirit has only one notion.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3598.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: as in the Trinity only the Son is called Word, only the Spirit is called Gift. What belongs to one person alone is proper to it.
claims: Only the Spirit is called Gift.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3601.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Gift' (donum) and 'given' (datum) differ in three ways. (1) In consignification: 'datum', a participle, co-signifies time, and 'donum', a noun, does not, so 'gift' fits timeless divine things better and can be eternal, while 'given' cannot. (2) In signification: donating adds to giving, since a gift is, according to the Philosopher, a giving not to be repaid, not one that cannot be repaid but one that seeks no repayment, so 'gift' implies liberality in the giver. (3) In mode of signifying: 'gift' implies aptitude for being given, 'given' actual giving. Aptitude can be passive, on the side of the thing given, as the heatable is apt for heating, or active, on the side of the giver, according to the ground on which something is given freely. The ground of every free bestowal is love, since what is given from cupidity or fear is not freely given but is rather gain or ransom. Since the Spirit is love, by the character of his procession he has both that he is given and that he is the ground of giving, so he is gift per se and first, and other things given are gifts only as they share something of love, being given from love. Combining these three features with the giver's authority over the gift, 'gift' in the Trinity belongs to the Spirit by his eternal procession, as he proceeds as love, the ground of free bestowal. As love is proper to him, so is 'gift'.
claims: 'Donum' differs from 'datum' by not co-signifying time, by implying liberality, and by signifying aptitude rather than act.
Love is the ground of all free giving, so the Spirit as love is gift per se and first.
'Gift' is proper to the Spirit by his eternal procession as love.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Gift' implies not actual mission but the ground of free bestowal or giving, which, though really the same as mission in the divine persons, differs conceptually. Although the Son is given or sent, the ground of free giving is love, the Spirit, and that ground does not belong to the Son, so he cannot properly be called gift, though he is called given.
claims: The Son is 'given' but not 'gift', since the ground of free giving is the Spirit as love.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3607.summary: Reply to the second argument. As shown in Distinction 13, the Son's procession is also named by its proper mode, generation, so his property, being Son, can be drawn from his proper procession. The Spirit's procession has no name for its proper mode, so from the personal act by which he is signified as proceeding one cannot draw what belongs to the mode of procession, as when he is called love or gift.
claims: Because the Spirit's procession lacks a proper name, 'gift' cannot be read off it as 'Son' is from generation.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3610.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Gift' or 'given', besides the relation by which it is so called, gives one to understand something given, though perhaps not as part of the name's signification, since the subject is not included in the signification of a name signifying an accident concretely (the Commentator; Avicenna held otherwise). It makes no difference to the concept of gift what genus the thing given is in. But as 'gift' is narrowed by the conditions described, the thing given must signify a relation, since gift as the ground of giving is love, and love can be given with authority held over it only as personal love, which is relative.
claims: The notional gift must be relative, since only personal love can be given with authority.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3614.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. As among essential attributes one common essence is goodness, wisdom, and the rest under different concepts, so among personal ones a single property differs only in its concepts as signified by different names. The property of the Word is signified one way by 'Son' and another by 'Word'. So the Spirit's property can be signified by different names under different concepts, and in our understanding one concept may follow another, as among essential attributes will presupposes intellect. In the same way the concept of gift follows that of love.
claims: One personal property can be signified under several concepts; 'gift' follows 'love' as will follows intellect.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3626.summary: First argument that not all gifts are given through the gift that is the Spirit. There is no alteration of alteration, or there would be an infinite regress (the Philosopher), so if a gift were given through a gift there would be a regress.
claims: There is no alteration of alteration.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3629.summary: Second argument. The divine essence is given by the Father to the Son (Hilary). If everything given were given through the Spirit, the essence would be given to the Son through the Spirit, making the Spirit a principle of the Son.
claims: The essence is given to the Son.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3632.summary: Third argument. The Son is also given to us (Isa. 9:6), and the Spirit has no character of principle relative to the Son.
claims: The Son is given to us.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3636.summary: Fourth argument. Nothing is given through a gift unless that gift is given, but many things are given us by God in which the Spirit is not given, such as natural gifts and freely given graces.
claims: The Spirit is not given in natural gifts.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3639.summary: Sed contra from Lombard's text. Also, the first in any genus is the cause of everything in that genus (the Philosopher), and the Spirit has the character of first gift, as the love of Father and Son, so all gifts are given through him.
claims: The first in a genus causes all in it.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3642.summary: Thomas's determination. Something is given in many ways. Sometimes from the very property of nature, as fire gives its heat and the sun its splendour, and will is not the principle of such giving. Sometimes from will as principle, and then either some benefit to the giver is intended, by removal of evil, as when something is given from fear, which is ransom, or by acquiring some good, which is gain or sale; or no benefit to the giver is intended, which is free giving and properly donation. Giving that intends the giver's benefit never fits God, so his alone is called free, since in all other givers some temporal or spiritual benefit to the giver is intended; no giving is purely free, as Avicenna says, except God's and his operation. The ground of free giving is love, which, according to Dionysius, moves higher things to provide for those that have less. Since the Spirit is love, he is the ground of all things given whose principle is the divine will, as are all things given to creatures.
claims: Only God's giving is purely free, seeking no benefit to the giver.
Love is the ground of free giving, so the Spirit is the ground of everything God gives to creatures.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3645.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Philosopher means that alteration does not terminate in alteration per se, not that one alteration cannot cause another. There is no infinite regress, since one reaches the first gift, which is given through itself and not through another gift of the Spirit.
claims: The regress of gifts ends in the first gift, given through itself.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3648.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Father's giving of the essence to the Son is giving from the property of nature, whose principle is nature, not will (Dist. 15), so it is not through the Spirit.
claims: The Father gives the essence to the Son by nature, not through the Spirit.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3651.summary: Reply to the third argument. Although the Spirit is not the principle of the Son, he is the principle of the effect by which the Son is said to be given or sent. So the Son too is given through the gift that is the Spirit, through love: 'God so loved the world that he gave his only Son' (John 3:16).
claims: The Son is given to the world through love, the Spirit.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3658.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Although all gifts, natural and gratuitous, are given us by God through love, the first gift, love itself is not given in all gifts, but only in the gift that is love's likeness, charity. When other gifts are said to be given through the gift of love, the Spirit, 'through' signifies not a cause on the recipient's side, as if by receiving the gift of love one received the others, but a causal relation on the giver's side, who gives everything given because he loves his creature.
claims: All gifts are given through love on the giver's side, but the Spirit himself is given only in charity.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3671.summary: First argument that the Spirit does not have by the same procession that he is God and that he is gift. The common and the proper do not have the same character, and 'gift' is proper to the Spirit while 'God' is common.
claims: Common and proper differ in character.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3674.summary: Second argument. Whatever the Spirit has by procession follows the procession in our understanding, but deity does not follow it, since it does not proceed, per se or per accidens, as it is not begotten.
claims: Deity does not proceed.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3677.summary: Sed contra. The Spirit is God only by having deity, and by procession he receives the whole deity from the Father, so by procession he is God.
claims: The Spirit receives deity by procession.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3681.summary: Thomas's determination. In the Son one can signify his property by way of relation ('filiation') or by way of going out or emanation ('passive generation' or 'nativity'). The same would hold of the Spirit if names had been coined, but for lack of names we use one name, 'procession', for both his emanation and his relation or property. Taken as relation or property, by his property the Spirit is formally Holy Spirit, gift, and love, but not God, as the Son is not formally God by filiation but Son by filiation, God by deity, and wise by wisdom. Taken as emanation, the Spirit is by his procession God and gift, as the Son by nativity is Son and God, but differently: deity relates to generation only as received through it, while filiation follows generation in our understanding. So the Son by being born received divinity, the gerund implying not mere concomitance ('he is a man by running') but ordering to what is received. Likewise with the Spirit's procession.
claims: As relation, the Spirit's procession makes him formally gift, not God; as emanation, by it he is both God and gift.
Deity is received through the procession, while the personal property follows it.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3684.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Spirit is not formally God and gift in the same respect, but he has both through the same emanation, since as the Son has nothing except what he received by being born, so the Spirit has nothing except what he received by proceeding.
claims: The Spirit receives everything, including deity, through his procession.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3687.summary: Reply to the second argument. The divine essence does not receive new being in the Spirit through procession, since the three persons have one and the same being, so it does not proceed, per se or per accidens, nor follow the procession; but the Spirit's having deity comes to him from his procession.
claims: The essence does not proceed, but the Spirit has it through procession.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3699.summary: First argument that the Spirit can be called 'our gift'. 'Gift' is said relative to creatures, and 'my' or 'our' can be added to names implying relation to creatures, as 'our Creator'.
claims: Relational names admit 'our'.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3702.summary: Second argument. 'Holy' takes nothing from the meaning of 'spirit', and we say 'our spirit', as 'the spirit of Elijah', so we can say 'our Holy Spirit'.
claims: 'Spirit' admits possessive pronouns.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3705.summary: Third argument. 'Son', like 'Father', implies an eternal relation from which it is imposed, and we say 'our Father', so we can say 'our Son'.
claims: We say 'our Father'.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3709.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is given to us is ours, and the Son was given to us, so he is our Son.
claims: What is given to us is ours.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3712.summary: Fifth argument. In God deity, God, wisdom, goodness, and the like are the same, and we say 'our God', so we can say 'God our wisdom' or 'our essence'.
claims: God, deity, and wisdom are identical in God.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3715.summary: Contrary argument that we cannot say 'our God'. The pronoun 'our' implies some relation of Creator to creature, but 'God' is an absolute name and a name of nature (Ambrose).
claims: 'Deus' is an absolute name of nature.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3718.summary: Thomas's determination. God can have a relation to us only as principle. Of the four causes, he is not our material cause; he relates to us as efficient, final, and exemplar formal cause, but not as inhering form. So divine names implying principle as efficient or final cause admit the possessive pronouns ('our Creator', 'our good'). Names said by way of inhering form do not, and all abstract divine names are signified as forms (essence, goodness), so we cannot say God is our essence or substance. Among these there is an order. Some abstract names imply efficient and exemplar principle, such as wisdom and goodness, and admit the pronouns causally: 'God is our wisdom', as he is 'our hope', because his wisdom produces in us a wisdom modelled on his, by which we are formally wise. Others imply principle only as exemplar, and the addition is not customary; we do not usually say God is our essence or substance. Yet sometimes it is made by reason of exemplarity, as Dionysius says the being of all things is the super-being of deity, though such expressions are to be explained rather than extended.
claims: God relates to us as efficient, final, and exemplar cause, never as inhering form.
Names of efficient or final principle admit 'our'; abstract names signifying form do not, except causally.
'God is our wisdom' is true causally; 'God is our essence' is not said, except by exemplarity.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3721.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Gift' implies an actual relation to the giver and, by its name, only an aptitudinal relation to the one it is given to. So it can always be called the giver's gift but is the recipient's only when actually given, which is why we say 'our given' (datum nostrum) but not 'our gift'.
claims: 'Gift' is always the giver's but is the recipient's only when actually given.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3724.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'Holy Spirit' is a circumlocution devised to express the person of the Spirit, and as a subsistent person he implies not the relation of principle but rather of one from a principle, so he cannot be called 'our Holy Spirit'. 'Spirit' implies the character of principle, since inspiration is from a spirit, so it can be called 'our spirit'.
claims: 'Spiritus Sanctus' names a person from a principle and so does not take 'our'; 'spiritus' does, as principle of inspiration.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3728.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Father' implies the character of principle and 'Son' does not, rather that of one from a principle, so the Son cannot be called 'our Son' as the Father is 'our Father'. Even 'our Father' is not said in the sense of eternal paternity, by which he is Father only of the natural Son.
claims: 'Our Father' is said by creation and adoption, not by eternal paternity.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3731.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Although the Son was given to us, he was not given to be our son but our teacher or saviour, so he can be called our Saviour but not our son. The argument 'he is Son and he is ours, so he is our Son' commits the fallacy of accident.
claims: The Son is given as our Saviour, not our son; the inference is a fallacy of accident.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3734.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Wisdom' in the abstract signifies that by which someone is formally wise, so for the reason given God cannot properly be said to be our wisdom except in the causal sense explained.
claims: Abstract names signify formal principles and so admit 'our' only causally.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3737.summary: Reply to the contrary argument. 'God', though it signifies the divine essence as to what it is imposed to signify, signifies an operation as to what it is imposed from (Damascene), so one can say 'our God'. God is said to be God of all and of the just differently. He is God of all by the relation of principle, as Creator of all. He is God of the just specially by the character of end, which they attain, and so he is said to be had by them. Other things are ordered to him as end but do not attain him, only the just, who are joined to him by grace and glory. So he is called end of all in common, but absolutely God 'of the just', who have him as their inheritance and in a kind of possession.
claims: 'Our God' is legitimate because 'Deus' is imposed from an operation.
God is God of all as Creator and specially of the just as the end they possess.

ta-l1d18q1-d1e3746.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'The relation does not appear in this name' seems false, since as 'gift' is said from giving, 'spirit' is from spiration. But 'spirit' implies a relation only accidentally, by its mode of signifying as the terminus of an action, while 'gift' implies a relation in its signification, since donating belongs to the genus of relation rather than action, giving being nothing but making one's own another's. Also 'spirit' is imposed to signify a substance by reason of a property, subtlety, as air and soul are called spirit, whereas 'gift' signifies not a substance but something about a substance that follows giving, so it is not reduced to the category of substance. (2) Hilary's 'not by defection, extension, or derivation is God from God' excludes three modes of emanation involving diversity of substance: generation from something corrupted (a worm from putrid flesh, air from water), production from something remaining joined (a branch from a tree), and production from something remaining but separated (a stream from a spring, fire from flint, and a human from a human). None fits the divine persons. The Son subsists by nativity from the power of nature, as formal principle of generation, in the same nature, the same not only in species but in number. (3) 'Not that spirit of ours by which we are': we exist in the Holy Spirit not formally but effectively; we are formally by our created spirit, the soul, and holy by the Holy Spirit effectively, and formally as we are sanctified by charity, the likeness of the love that is the Spirit, by which the Spirit is joined to us. (4) 'I will take of your spirit' (Num. 11:17) does not mean that Moses' grace was diminished in its habit but in its exercise of care, with others appointed to help him. It is called 'of his spirit' not because the Spirit's person is divisible or a habit of grace can be transferred and divided, but because they received lesser grace than Moses for similar acts, as if propagated from his, since he obtained it for them by prayer. (5) The question whether the Spirit is related to himself is answered in Distinction 30.
claims: 'Gift' signifies a relation in its very meaning, while 'spirit' does only accidentally.
Hilary excludes emanation by corruption, extension, or separation; the Son subsists by nativity in numerically the same nature.
We are holy by the Spirit effectively and by charity, his likeness, formally.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 18 introduces the name 'gift' as fitting the Spirit by reason of his procession and its contrast with 'given'. It notes that the Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given, and announces five articles on the name 'gift'.
claims: The Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3533.summary: Article 1 asks whether 'gift' is essential or personal. Distinguishing giving with authority of principle from giving as free possession, Thomas holds that 'gift' is notional when it implies the giver's authority and essential when it implies only free possession, as the essence is 'given' to the Son. 'Gift' connotes an effect in creatures but also a relation to an authoritative principle, as 'assuming flesh' connotes a common operation with a proper terminus. Essential love and what remains when the persons are abstracted are not gift in the notional sense.
claims: 'Gift' is notional when implying authority of origin, essential when implying only free possession.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3577.summary: Article 2 asks whether 'gift' is proper to the Spirit. Thomas distinguishes 'donum' from 'datum' by consignification of time, by liberality, and by aptitude versus act. Since love is the ground of all free giving, the Spirit, proceeding as love, is gift per se and first, and 'gift' is proper to him by his eternal procession, as love is. The Son is 'given' but not 'gift'. 'Gift' cannot be read off the Spirit's procession because that procession lacks a proper name, and one property can be signified by several concepts, with 'gift' following 'love'.
claims: 'Gift' is proper to the Spirit, since he proceeds as love, the ground of free giving.
The Son is given but not gift.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3618.summary: Article 3 asks whether all gifts are given through the gift that is the Spirit. Thomas distinguishes giving by nature from giving by will, and among the latter ransom and sale from free donation, which alone fits God. Since love is the ground of free giving, the Spirit is the ground of everything God gives to creatures, including the Son's being given to the world. The regress ends in the first gift. The Father gives the essence to the Son by nature, not through the Spirit, and the Spirit himself is given only in charity, 'through' marking causality on the giver's side.
claims: All gifts to creatures are given through love, the Spirit, though he himself is given only in charity.
Only God's giving is purely free.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3663.summary: Article 4 asks whether by the procession by which he is gift the Spirit is also God. 'Procession' names both the Spirit's emanation and his relation. As relation, it makes him formally gift and love but not God, since he is God by deity. As emanation, by it he is both God and gift, since he receives deity through it, as the Son received divinity by being born, though the essence itself does not proceed.
claims: By his procession as emanation the Spirit receives deity; by his property he is formally gift.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3691.summary: Article 5 asks whether the Spirit can be called 'our gift'. God relates to us as efficient, final, and exemplar cause, never as inhering form, so names of efficient or final principle take 'our' while abstract names take it only causally ('God our wisdom'). 'Gift' is the giver's but the recipient's only when given, hence 'our given', not 'our gift'. 'Holy Spirit' and 'Son', naming persons from a principle, do not take 'our', and 'our God' is legitimate because 'God' is imposed from an operation. God is God of all as Creator and God of the just as their possessed end.
claims: The Spirit is 'our given' but not 'our gift'.
Divine names take possessive pronouns only when they imply efficient or final principle.

ta-l1d18q1-Dd1e3741.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 18 explains that 'gift' signifies a relation in its very meaning, unlike 'spirit'. It interprets Hilary's exclusion of three modes of emanation from the divine processions, distinguishes being holy by the Spirit effectively from being holy by charity formally, and glosses the spirit taken from Moses.
claims: 'Gift' is a relational name; we are holy by the Spirit effectively and by charity formally.

ta-l1d18q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 18 treats the name 'gift' as said of the Spirit. Article 1 holds that 'gift' is notional when it implies the giver's authority of origin and essential when it implies only free possession. Article 2 holds that 'gift' is proper to the Spirit by his eternal procession, since he proceeds as love, the ground of all free giving, and distinguishes 'donum' (aptitude, liberality, timeless) from 'datum' (actual, temporal). The Son is given but not gift. Article 3 holds that everything God gives creatures, including the Son, is given through love, the Spirit, God's giving alone being purely free, though the Spirit himself is given only in charity. Article 4 holds that by his procession as emanation the Spirit receives deity, while his relation makes him formally gift. Article 5 analyses possessive pronouns with divine names, concluding that the Spirit is 'our given' but not 'our gift', and that God is specially God of the just.
claims: 'Gift' is the Spirit's proper name, since he proceeds as love, the ground of all free giving.
Everything God gives creatures is given through love; only God gives purely freely.
The Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given, 'our given' but not 'our gift'.
